title: OPIC: Enhancing Language Model Merging via Optimizing In-Context Capability
claim: Merging degrades in-context learning capability, and restoring it without changing task knowledge recovers downstream performance, so ICL capability tracks merging quality.
layout: 3 panels: top conceptual scatter, bottom two bar charts; hand-drawn sketch style
description: A hand-drawn, sketch-style figure with three panels. The top panel is a conceptual scatter with ICL-capability on the y-axis and average-performance on the x-axis. A large circle (pre-trained model) sits at upper left. A red arrow runs down to a square (merged model) at the bottom middle. A second arrow runs up and right to a diamond (prompt-tuned model). A teal-bordered legend box in the top right maps the shapes to model types. Below it are two bar charts separated by a dashed red vertical line. The left chart shows AVG-SCORE for the three shapes (70.1, 72.6, 76.6), with double-headed arrows to a dashed FT line above them. The right chart shows REG-SCORE (0.86, 0.73, 0.79), with curved arrows linking the bars. The palette is cream, teal and dark red.
caption: Evaluating the correlation between in-context learning (ICL) capability and merging performance. Four tasks are merged into Qwen1.5-7B via Task Arithmetic, followed by Soft Prompt Tuning with DROID to enhance ICL without modifying parameters or task knowledge. Performance is assessed on REGBench and downstream tasks.
abstract: Task-vector–based model merging enables low-cost, training-free multi-task learning for large language models, but suffers from severe performance degradation due to task conflict. Prior mitigation strategies largely rely on validation data for costly hyperparameter tuning, limiting both interpretability and practicality. We therefore propose OPIC, an evolutionary optimization–based model merging framework. Our preliminary experiments reveal that the degradation of In-Context Learning (ICL) capabilities is a primary driver of task conflict. Motivated by this insight, we formulate model merging as an optimization problem with ICL preservation as the objective. OPIC introduces a hierarchical refinement operators and optimizes it using self-generated data, effectively eliminating the reliance on external validation sets. Experimental results demonstrate that OPIC achieves an average performance retention of 80.73%, outperforming SOTA methods and improving by up to 11.1% over recent validation-free approaches. In addition, OPIC is compatible with existing merging pipelines, offering a new alternative solution for deploying without validation dependencies. Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OPIC-CFFE.
